# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-serif)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--color-text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--border-radius-md)` (or `-lg` for cards) in HTML. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - Scripts execute after streaming — load libraries via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` (UMD globals), then use the global in a plain `<script>` that follows. - **CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external resources may ONLY load from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`, `fonts.googleapis.com`, `fonts.gstatic.com`. All other origins are blocked by the sandbox — the request silently fails. ### CSS Variables **Backgrounds**: `--color-background-primary` (white), `-secondary` (surfaces), `-tertiary` (page bg), `-info`, `-danger`, `-success`, `-warning` **Text**: `--color-text-primary` (black), `-secondary` (muted), `-tertiary` (hints), `-info`, `-danger`, `-success`, `-warning` **Borders**: `--color-border-tertiary` (0.15α, default), `-secondary` (0.3α, hover), `-primary` (0.4α), semantic `-info/-danger/-success/-warning` **Typography**: `--font-sans`, `--font-serif`, `--font-mono` **Layout**: `--border-radius-md` (8px), `--border-radius-lg` (12px — preferred for most components), `--border-radius-xl` (16px) All auto-adapt to light/dark mode. For custom colors in HTML, use CSS variables. **Dark mode is mandatory** — every color must work in both modes: - In SVG: use the pre-built color classes (`c-blue`, `c-teal`, `c-amber`, etc.) for colored nodes — they handle light/dark mode automatically. Never write `<style>` blocks for colors. - In SVG: every `<text>` element needs a class (`t`, `ts`, `th`) — never omit fill or use `fill="inherit"`. Inside a `c-{color}` parent, text classes auto-adjust to the ramp. - In HTML: always use CSS variables (--color-text-primary, --color-text-secondary) for text. Never hardcode colors like color: #333 — invisible in dark mode. - Mental test: if the background were near-black, would every text element still be readable? ### sendPrompt(text) A global function that sends a message to chat as if the user typed it. Use it when the user's next step benefits from Claude thinking. Handle filtering, sorting, toggling, and calculations in JS instead. ### Links `<a href="https://...">` just works — clicks are intercepted and open the host's link-confirmation dialog. Or call `openLink(url)` directly. ## When nothing fits Pick the closest use case below and adapt. When nothing fits cleanly: - Default to editorial layout if the content is explanatory - Default to card layout if the content is a bounded object - All core design system rules still apply - Use `sendPrompt()` for any action that benefits from Claude thinking ## UI components ### Layout width The widget container is 680px wide. Use `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(160px, 1fr))` for responsive columns — auto-fit lets the grid pick column count by available width. ### Aesthetic Flat, clean, white surfaces. Minimal 0.5px borders. Generous whitespace. No gradients, no shadows (except functional focus rings). Everything should feel native to claude.ai — like it belongs on the page, not embedded from somewhere else. ### Tokens - Borders: always `0.5px solid var(--color-border-tertiary)` (or `-secondary` for emphasis) - Corner radius: `var(--border-radius-md)` for most elements, `var(--border-radius-lg)` for cards - Cards: white bg (`var(--color-background-primary)`), 0.5px border, radius-lg, padding 1rem 1.25rem - Form elements (input, select, textarea, button, range slider) are pre-styled — write bare tags. Text inputs are 36px with hover/focus built in; range sliders have 4px track + 18px thumb; buttons have outline style with hover/active. Only add inline styles to override (e.g., different width). - Buttons: pre-styled with transparent bg, 0.5px border-secondary, hover bg-secondary, active scale(0.98). If it triggers sendPrompt, append a ↗ arrow. - **Round every displayed number.** JS float math leaks artifacts — `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`, `7 * 1.1` gives `7.700000000000001`. Any number that reaches the screen (slider readouts, stat card values, axis labels, data-point labels, tooltips, computed totals) must go through `Math.round()`, `.toFixed(n)`, or `Intl.NumberFormat`. Pick the precision that makes sense for the context — integers for counts, 1–2 decimals for percentages, `toLocaleString()` for currency. For range sliders, also set `step="1"` (or step="0.1" etc.) so the input itself emits round values. - Spacing: use rem for vertical rhythm (1rem, 1.5rem, 2rem), px for component-internal gaps (8px, 12px, 16px) - Box-shadows: none, except `box-shadow: 0 0 0 Npx` focus rings on inputs ### Metric cards For summary numbers (revenue, count, percentage) — surface card with muted 13px label above, 24px/500 number below. `background: var(--color-background-secondary)`, no border, `border-radius: var(--border-radius-md)`, padding 1rem. Use in grids of 2-4 with `gap: 12px`. Distinct from raised cards (which have white bg + border). ### Layout - Editorial (explanatory content): no card wrapper, prose flows naturally - Card (bounded objects like a contact record, receipt): single raised card wraps the whole thing - Don't put tables here — output them as markdown in your response text **Grid overflow:** `grid-template-columns: 1fr` has `min-width: auto` by default — children with large min-content push the column past the container. Use `minmax(0, 1fr)` to clamp. **Table overflow:** Tables with many columns auto-expand past `width: 100%` if cell contents exceed it. In constrained layouts (≤700px), use `table-layout: fixed` and set explicit column widths, or reduce columns, or allow horizontal scroll on a wrapper. ### Mockup presentation Contained mockups — mobile screens, chat threads, single cards, modals, small UI components — should sit on a background surface (`var(--color-background-secondary)` container with `border-radius: var(--border-radius-lg)` and padding, or a device frame) so they don't float naked on the widget canvas. Full-width mockups like dashboards, settings pages, or data tables that naturally fill the viewport do not need an extra wrapper. ### 1. Interactive explainer — learn how something works *"Explain how compound interest works" / "Teach me about sorting algorithms"* Use HTML for the interactive controls — sliders, buttons, live state displays, charts. Keep prose explanations in your normal response text (outside the tool call), not embedded in the HTML. No card wrapper. Whitespace is the container. ```html <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <label style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--color-text-secondary);">Years</label> <input type="range" min="1" max="40" value="20" id="years" style="flex: 1;" /> <span style="font-size: 14px; font-weight: 500; min-width: 24px;" id="years-out">20</span> </div> <div style="display: flex; align-items: baseline; gap: 8px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <span style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--color-text-secondary);">£1,000 →</span> <span style="font-size: 24px; font-weight: 500;" id="result">£3,870</span> </div> <div style="margin: 2rem 0; position: relative; height: 240px;"> <canvas id="chart"></canvas> </div> ``` Use `sendPrompt()` to let users ask follow-ups: `sendPrompt('What if I increase the rate to 10%?')` ### 2. Compare options — decision making *"Compare pricing and features of these products" / "Help me choose between React and Vue"* Use HTML. Side-by-side card grid for options. Highlight differences with semantic colors. Interactive elements for filtering or weighting. - Each option in a card. Use badges for key differentiators. A leading Tabler icon (`<i class="ti ti-NAME">` at 20px, `aria-hidden`) anchors each option visually — pick the most apt name per option. - Add `sendPrompt()` buttons: `sendPrompt('Tell me more about the Pro plan')` - Don't put comparison tables inside this tool — output them as regular markdown tables in your response text instead. The tool is for the visual card grid only. - When one option is recommended or "most popular", accent its card with `border: 2px solid var(--color-border-info)` only (2px is deliberate — the only exception to the 0.5px rule, used to accent featured items) — keep the same background and border as the other cards. Add a small badge (e.g. "Most popular") above or inside the card header using `background: var(--color-background-info); color: var(--color-text-info); font-size: 12px; padding: 4px 12px; border-radius: var(--border-radius-md)`. ### 3. Data record — bounded UI object *"Show me a Salesforce contact card" / "Create a receipt for this order"* Use HTML. Wrap the entire thing in a single raised card. All content is sans-serif since it's pure UI. Use an avatar/initials circle for people (see example below). ```html <div style="background: var(--color-background-primary); border-radius: var(--border-radius-lg); border: 0.5px solid var(--color-border-tertiary); padding: 1rem 1.25rem;"> <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 16px;"> <div style="width: 44px; height: 44px; border-radius: 50%; background: var(--color-background-info); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; font-weight: 500; font-size: 14px; color: var(--color-text-info);">MR</div> <div> <p style="font-weight: 500; font-size: 15px; margin: 0;">Maya Rodriguez</p> <p style="font-size: 13px; color: var(--color-text-secondary); margin: 0;">VP of Engineering</p> </div> </div> <div style="border-top: 0.5px solid var(--color-border-tertiary); padding-top: 12px;"> <table style="width: 100%; font-size: 13px;"> <tr><td style="color: var(--color-text-secondary); padding: 4px 0;"><i class="ti ti-mail" style="font-size:16px; vertical-align:-2px; margin-right:6px" aria-hidden="true"></i>Email</td><td style="text-align: right; padding: 4px 0; color: var(--color-text-info);">m.rodriguez@acme.com</td></tr> <tr><td style="color: var(--color-text-secondary); padding: 4px 0;"><i class="ti ti-phone" style="font-size:16px; vertical-align:-2px; margin-right:6px" aria-hidden="true"></i>Phone</td><td style="text-align: right; padding: 4px 0;">+1 (415) 555-0172</td></tr> </table> </div> </div> ``` ## Color palette 9 color ramps, each with 7 stops from lightest to darkest. 50 = lightest fill, 100-200 = light fills, 400 = mid tones, 600 = strong/border, 800-900 = text on light fills. | Class | Ramp | 50 (lightest) | 100 | 200 | 400 | 600 | 800 | 900 (darkest) | |-------|------|------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|------| | `c-purple` | Purple | #EEEDFE | #CECBF6 | #AFA9EC | #7F77DD | #534AB7 | #3C3489 | #26215C | | `c-teal` | Teal | #E1F5EE | #9FE1CB | #5DCAA5 | #1D9E75 | #0F6E56 | #085041 | #04342C | | `c-coral` | Coral | #FAECE7 | #F5C4B3 | #F0997B | #D85A30 | #993C1D | #712B13 | #4A1B0C | | `c-pink` | Pink | #FBEAF0 | #F4C0D1 | #ED93B1 | #D4537E | #993556 | #72243E | #4B1528 | | `c-gray` | Gray | #F1EFE8 | #D3D1C7 | #B4B2A9 | #888780 | #5F5E5A | #444441 | #2C2C2A | | `c-blue` | Blue | #E6F1FB | #B5D4F4 | #85B7EB | #378ADD | #185FA5 | #0C447C | #042C53 | | `c-green` | Green | #EAF3DE | #C0DD97 | #97C459 | #639922 | #3B6D11 | #27500A | #173404 | | `c-amber` | Amber | #FAEEDA | #FAC775 | #EF9F27 | #BA7517 | #854F0B | #633806 | #412402 | | `c-red` | Red | #FCEBEB | #F7C1C1 | #F09595 | #E24B4A | #A32D2D | #791F1F | #501313 | **How to assign colors**: Color should encode meaning, not sequence. Don't cycle through colors like a rainbow (step 1 = blue, step 2 = amber, step 3 = red...). Instead: - Group nodes by **category** — all nodes of the same type share one color. E.g. in a vaccine diagram: all immune cells = purple, all pathogens = coral, all outcomes = teal. - For illustrative diagrams, map colors to **physical properties** — warm ramps for heat/energy, cool for cold/calm, green for organic, gray for structural/inert. - Use **gray for neutral/structural** nodes (start, end, generic steps). - Use **2-3 colors per diagram**, not 6+. More colors = more visual noise. A diagram with gray + purple + teal is cleaner than one using every ramp. - **Prefer purple, teal, coral, pink** for general diagram categories. Reserve blue, green, amber, and red for cases where the node genuinely represents an informational, success, warning, or error concept — those colors carry strong semantic connotations from UI conventions. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use blue/amber/red freely when they map to physical properties like temperature or pressure.) **Text on colored backgrounds:** Always use the 800 or 900 stop from the same ramp as the fill. Here's a comprehensive guide to gathering dog emotional sound data for your model, covering all three emotions — **alert**, **bored**, and **playful**.

---

## 🐶 Dog Emotion Sound Datasets for ML Training

### What Sounds to Look For Per Emotion

| Emotion | Typical Sounds |
|---|---|
| **Alert** | Short, sharp barks; low growls; stiff whines; rapid repeated barks |
| **Bored** | Long drawn-out whines; yawning sounds; low moaning; intermittent single barks |
| **Playful** | High-pitched yips; excited rapid barking; play growls; short squeaky barks |

---

### 🗂️ Ready-Made Datasets

**1. Abzaliev / Mescalina Bark Dataset (Best for your use case)**
This dataset contains 8,034 dog vocalizations across 14 call-types, including normal, aggressive, fearful, and playful barks, vocalizations related to owner interaction, whines, growls, and barks associated with sadness or anxiety. Recordings come from Chihuahuas, French Poodles, and Schnauzers. It maps well to alert and playful — look it up on GitHub/arXiv (search "Abzaliev dog bark dataset").

**2. LingChongTong Pet Vocalization Dataset**
This large-scale dataset contains 42,553 audio samples with 8 emotion categories including alert (12.5%), playful (4.2%), excited (7.8%), anxious, territorial, and others. All samples are in WAV format at 44.1 kHz with 1–5 second durations, annotated by veterinary behaviorists. This is very close to what you need.

**3. Kaggle: Dog Voice Emotion Dataset**
Available at `kaggle.com/datasets/shivarao100/dog-voice-emotion-dataset` — a demo-lite dataset with labeled dog emotion audio clips.

**4. DogSpeak Dataset (Hugging Face)**
DogSpeak is available on Hugging Face (`ArlingtonCL2/DogSpeak_Dataset`) and contains 77,202 bark sequences in WAV format from 156 individual dogs across 5 breeds. It's sourced from real-world online videos for natural, in-the-wild variety.

---

### 🔊 Free Audio Sources to Manually Collect & Label

Since "bored" is underrepresented in most datasets, you may need to supplement:

- **Freesound.org** — search "dog whine", "dog bored", "dog yawn", "dog playful bark", "dog alert bark". Has Creative Commons audio you can download and label.
- **Pixabay** — royalty-free dog sounds requiring no attribution, available as MP3 downloads.
- **YouTube** — search "dog sounds bored compilation", "dog alert barking", "dog playing sounds" and extract audio with `yt-dlp`.

---

### 🛠️ Suggested Pipeline

```
1. Download datasets above (Abzaliev, LingChongTong, Kaggle)
2. Filter/relabel to your 3 classes: alert / bored / playful
3. Supplement "bored" samples from Freesound.org (least common in datasets)
4. Convert all to WAV, 16kHz or 22kHz mono
5. Extract features: MFCCs, mel spectrograms, chroma
6. Train classifier (e.g., CNN on spectrograms or SVM on MFCCs)
```

---

### 💡 Tips for "Bored" Sounds Specifically

Bored is the hardest class to find labeled. Look for:
- Long, low-pitched single whines
- Yawning + lip-smacking sounds
- Slow, monotone repeated barks

### 2.2 Dog Vocalizations Extraction

The original audios downloaded from YouTube contain long uninformative segments where dogs are silent or background noises muffling the vocalizations. To ensure the quality of our dataset, we have adopted a systematic and rigorous pipeline of three steps to extract pure and singular vocal segments from the audios.

Step 1: sentence-level segmentations extraction As a preliminary step, we extract long segments in which contains a continuous series of dog vocalizations. Such long segments, which we call a dog "sentence", can be detected because they are preceded or followed by significant periods of silence. We apply PANNs (Kong et al. 2020), a pre-trained large sound event detection model including as many as 527 sound classes for recognizing the sound events. The continous segments detected by PANNs with the event class "barking" are considered as the sentence-level bark segmentations.

Here's a comprehensive guide to gathering dog emotional sound data for your model, covering all three emotions — **alert**, **bored**, and **playful**.

---

## 🐶 Dog Emotion Sound Datasets for ML Training

### What Sounds to Look For Per Emotion

| Emotion | Typical Sounds |
|---|---|
| **Alert** | Short, sharp barks; low growls; stiff whines; rapid repeated barks |
| **Bored** | Long drawn-out whines; yawning sounds; low moaning; intermittent single barks |
| **Playful** | High-pitched yips; excited rapid barking; play growls; short squeaky barks |

---

### 🗂️ Ready-Made Datasets

**1. Abzaliev / Mescalina Bark Dataset (Best for your use case)**
This dataset contains 8,034 dog vocalizations across 14 call-types, including normal, aggressive, fearful, and playful barks, vocalizations related to owner interaction, whines, growls, and barks associated with sadness or anxiety. Recordings come from Chihuahuas, French Poodles, and Schnauzers. It maps well to alert and playful — look it up on GitHub/arXiv (search "Abzaliev dog bark dataset").

**2. LingChongTong Pet Vocalization Dataset**
This large-scale dataset contains 42,553 audio samples with 8 emotion categories including alert (12.5%), playful (4.2%), excited (7.8%), anxious, territorial, and others. All samples are in WAV format at 44.1 kHz with 1–5 second durations, annotated by veterinary behaviorists. This is very close to what you need.

**3. Kaggle: Dog Voice Emotion Dataset**
Available at `kaggle.com/datasets/shivarao100/dog-voice-emotion-dataset` — a demo-lite dataset with labeled dog emotion audio clips.

**4. DogSpeak Dataset (Hugging Face)**
DogSpeak is available on Hugging Face (`ArlingtonCL2/DogSpeak_Dataset`) and contains 77,202 bark sequences in WAV format from 156 individual dogs across 5 breeds. It's sourced from real-world online videos for natural, in-the-wild variety.

---

### 🔊 Free Audio Sources to Manually Collect & Label

Since "bored" is underrepresented in most datasets, you may need to supplement:

- **Freesound.org** — search "dog whine", "dog bored", "dog yawn", "dog playful bark", "dog alert bark". Has Creative Commons audio you can download and label.
- **Pixabay** — royalty-free dog sounds requiring no attribution, available as MP3 downloads.
- **YouTube** — search "dog sounds bored compilation", "dog alert barking", "dog playing sounds" and extract audio with `yt-dlp`.

---

### 🛠️ Suggested Pipeline

```
1. Download datasets above (Abzaliev, LingChongTong, Kaggle)
2. Filter/relabel to your 3 classes: alert / bored / playful
3. Supplement "bored" samples from Freesound.org (least common in datasets)
4. Convert all to WAV, 16kHz or 22kHz mono
5. Extract features: MFCCs, mel spectrograms, chroma
6. Train classifier (e.g., CNN on spectrograms or SVM on MFCCs)
```

---

### 💡 Tips for "Bored" Sounds Specifically

Bored is the hardest class to find labeled. Look for:
- Long, low-pitched single whines
- Yawning + lip-smacking sounds
- Slow, monotone repeated barks

Search Freesound with tags like `dog-whine`, `dog-bored`, `dog-attention-seeking`.

Here's a full breakdown of the approach and how to use it.

---

## Architecture: 3-Layer Detection Pipeline

The core insight is that audio leakage manifests in three distinct forms, each requiring a different mathematical detector:

### Layer 1 — SHA-256 Exact Hash
Catches **bitwise duplicates** — files that are literally the same bytes under different filenames. Zero false positives, O(n) cost. Always runs first to prune the candidate set.

### Layer 2 — Spectral Fingerprint (MFCC + Chroma + ZCR)
Catches **same-source slices** — chunks cut from the same recording that share the same acoustic content. The fingerprint vector is:

```
[MFCC_mean(40) | MFCC_std(40) | Chroma_mean(12) | Chroma_std(12) | ZCR_mean(1)]
```

L2-normalized, then compared via **cosine similarity**. Same-source slices score ≥ 0.97; unrelated speech ≤ 0.85. You can tune `--sim_threshold` if your data is noisier.

### Layer 3 — Noise Floor Fingerprint
Catches the subtler case: **different speech content from the same recording session**. It isolates the 0–300 Hz sub-band (where stationary room/mic noise lives), takes the **10th-percentile power across time frames** (speech-free frames dominate), and compares those spectra. Files recorded with the same mic in the same room share a near-identical noise signature even when the words are different.

### Union-Find for Transitive Grouping
Once pairs are flagged by Layers 2/3, a **Union-Find structure** groups them transitively — if A≈B and B≈C, all three are in one group. The alphabetically-first file in each group is kept; the rest move to trash.

---

## Usage

**Install dependencies:**
```bash
pip install librosa numpy scipy scikit-learn tqdm
```

**Recommended first run — dry run with report:**
```bash
python detect_audio_leakage.py --dry_run --report
```
This shows you exactly what would be moved without touching anything.

**Full run:**
```bash
python detect_audio_leakage.py --report
```

**Tune thresholds if needed:**
```bash
# More aggressive — catches more potential leaks
python detect_audio_leakage.py --sim_threshold 0.95 --noise_threshold 0.94 --report

# More conservative — only very obvious duplicates
python detect_audio_leakage.py --sim_threshold 0.99 --noise_threshold 0.98 --report
```

---

## After Cleaning

Before retraining, validate the cleanup worked:

input.file_text:
"""
Audio Data Leakage Detector — Anxiety Class Deduplication
==========================================================
Detects and quarantines duplicate/source-leaked audio chunks using a
3-layer detection pipeline:

  Layer 1 — Exact SHA-256 hash match (bitwise duplicates)
  Layer 2 — Spectral fingerprinting via MFCC + chroma cosine similarity
             (same source, different slice offsets / minor re-encodings)
  Layer 3 — Background noise fingerprint clustering via low-energy band
             correlation (same recording session, different content)

For each group of duplicates/source-leaks, ONE representative file is kept
(the first alphabetically) and the rest are moved to Anxiety_Trash/.

Usage:
    python detect_audio_leakage.py [--input_dir PATH] [--output_dir PATH]
                                   [--sim_threshold FLOAT] [--noise_threshold FLOAT]
                                   [--dry_run] [--report]

Dependencies:
    pip install librosa numpy scipy scikit-learn tqdm
"""

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import logging
import shutil
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import librosa
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import cosine
from sklearn.preprocessing import normalize
from tqdm import tqdm

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# CONFIG DEFAULTS
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEFAULT_INPUT_DIR   = "Outputs/Clean_Emotion_Data/Anxiety"
DEFAULT_TRASH_DIR   = "Outputs/Clean_Emotion_Data/Anxiety_Trash"
SR                  = 16_000          # expected sample rate
CHUNK_DURATION      = 3.0             # seconds

# Layer 2 — spectral fingerprint similarity
#   1.0 = identical, 0.0 = orthogonal
#   Empirically: same-source slices score ≥ 0.97, unrelated ≤ 0.85
SPECTRAL_SIM_THRESHOLD  = 0.97

# Layer 3 — background noise band (Hz) used for session fingerprinting
NOISE_LOW_HZ            = 0
NOISE_HIGH_HZ           = 300        # sub-300 Hz captures room/mic noise
NOISE_SIM_THRESHOLD     = 0.96       # cosine sim on noise band spectrum

# MFCC config — 40 coefficients gives good spectro-temporal resolution
N_MFCC                  = 40
# Chroma captures harmonic content independent of timbre
N_CHROMA                = 12


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LOGGING
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
)
log = logging.getLogger("leakage_detector")


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LAYER 1 — SHA-256 EXACT HASH
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def sha256(path: Path) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()


def find_exact_duplicates(files: list[Path]) -> dict[str, list[Path]]:
    """Group files by identical SHA-256 hash."""
    hash_map: dict[str, list[Path]] = defaultdict(list)
    log.info("Layer 1 — computing SHA-256 hashes …")
    for p in tqdm(files, desc="Hashing", unit="file"):
        hash_map[sha256(p)].append(p)
    return {h: paths for h, paths in hash_map.items() if len(paths) > 1}


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# AUDIO LOADING UTILITY
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def load_audio(path: Path) -> np.ndarray | None:
    try:
        y, _ = librosa.load(path, sr=SR, mono=True, duration=CHUNK_DURATION)
        # Pad/trim to exact length
        target = int(SR * CHUNK_DURATION)
        if len(y) < target:
            y = np.pad(y, (0, target - len(y)))
        else:
            y = y[:target]
        return y
    except Exception as e:
        log.warning(f"Could not load {path.name}: {e}")
        return None


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LAYER 2 — SPECTRAL FINGERPRINT (MFCC + CHROMA)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def spectral_fingerprint(y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Concatenate mean+std of MFCC and chroma features into a fixed-length
    vector.  This is robust to minor re-encoding / codec differences while
    being sensitive enough to distinguish different speech content.
    """
    # MFCC — captures spectral envelope (timbre / phoneme identity)
    mfcc = librosa.feature.mfcc(y=y, sr=SR, n_mfcc=N_MFCC)         # (40, T)
    mfcc_mean = mfcc.mean(axis=1)                                     # (40,)
    mfcc_std  = mfcc.std(axis=1)                                      # (40,)

    # Chroma — captures tonal/harmonic content
    chroma = librosa.feature.chroma_stft(y=y, sr=SR, n_chroma=N_CHROMA) # (12, T)
    chroma_mean = chroma.mean(axis=1)                                  # (12,)
    chroma_std  = chroma.std(axis=1)                                   # (12,)

    # Zero-crossing rate mean — crude speech/silence indicator
    zcr_mean = librosa.feature.zero_crossing_rate(y).mean(keepdims=True)

    vec = np.concatenate([mfcc_mean, mfcc_std, chroma_mean, chroma_std, zcr_mean])
    # L2-normalize so cosine distance == euclidean distance on unit sphere
    return normalize(vec.reshape(1, -1), norm="l2").ravel()


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LAYER 3 — BACKGROUND NOISE FINGERPRINT
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def noise_fingerprint(y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Capture the low-frequency (≤300 Hz) power spectrum as a noise fingerprint.
    Files recorded in the same session with the same mic/room share a nearly
    identical stationary noise floor, even if the speech content differs.
    """
    n_fft = 2048
    S = np.abs(librosa.stft(y, n_fft=n_fft))           # (n_fft/2+1, T)
    freqs = librosa.fft_frequencies(sr=SR, n_fft=n_fft) # (n_fft/2+1,)

    # Isolate noise band
    band_mask = (freqs >= NOISE_LOW_HZ) & (freqs <= NOISE_HIGH_HZ)
    noise_band = S[band_mask, :]                          # (B, T)

    # Take the 10th-percentile power across time — this picks the
    # quietest (speech-free) frames, revealing the stationary noise floor
    noise_floor = np.percentile(noise_band, 10, axis=1)  # (B,)
    return normalize(noise_floor.reshape(1, -1), norm="l2").ravel()


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# SIMILARITY CHECK HELPERS
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def cosine_sim(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Returns cosine similarity in [0, 1]."""
    return float(1.0 - cosine(a, b))


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# UNION-FIND for transitive duplicate grouping
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class UnionFind:
    def __init__(self, n: int):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank   = [0] * n

    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, x: int, y: int):
        rx, ry = self.find(x), self.find(y)
        if rx == ry:
            return
        if self.rank[rx] < self.rank[ry]:
            rx, ry = ry, rx
        self.parent[ry] = rx
        if self.rank[rx] == self.rank[ry]:
            self.rank[rx] += 1

    def groups(self) -> dict[int, list[int]]:
        from collections import defaultdict
        d: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
        for i in range(len(self.parent)):
            d[self.find(i)].append(i)
        return {k: v for k, v in d.items() if len(v) > 1}


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# MAIN PIPELINE
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def detect_leakage(
    input_dir: Path,
    trash_dir: Path,
    spectral_threshold: float,
    noise_threshold: float,
    dry_run: bool,
    report: bool,
) -> dict:
    # ── Gather files ──────────────────────────────────────────
    files = sorted(input_dir.glob("*.wav"))
    if not files:
        log.error(f"No .wav files found in {input_dir}")
        sys.exit(1)
    log.info(f"Found {len(files)} .wav files in {input_dir}")

    to_move: set[Path] = set()
    report_data: dict = {
        "total_files"       : len(files),
        "exact_duplicates"  : [],
        "spectral_duplicates": [],
        "noise_duplicates"  : [],
        "files_moved"       : [],
    }

    # ── LAYER 1: Exact hashes ─────────────────────────────────
    exact_groups = find_exact_duplicates(files)
    log.info(f"Layer 1: {len(exact_groups)} exact-duplicate group(s) found")
    for digest, group in exact_groups.items():
        keep = sorted(group)[0]
        dupes = sorted(group)[1:]
        log.info(f"  EXACT group ({digest[:12]}…): keep={keep.name}, "
                 f"remove={[p.name for p in dupes]}")
        report_data["exact_duplicates"].append({
            "keep": keep.name,
            "duplicates": [p.name for p in dupes],
        })
        to_move.update(dupes)

    # ── Load audio + compute fingerprints ────────────────────
    log.info("Loading audio and computing fingerprints …")
    audio_map:    dict[Path, np.ndarray] = {}
    spec_fp_map:  dict[Path, np.ndarray] = {}
    noise_fp_map: dict[Path, np.ndarray] = {}

    for p in tqdm(files, desc="Fingerprinting", unit="file"):
        if p in to_move:
            continue   # skip already-flagged exact dupes
        y = load_audio(p)
        if y is None:
            continue
        audio_map[p]    = y
        spec_fp_map[p]  = spectral_fingerprint(y)
        noise_fp_map[p] = noise_fingerprint(y)

    remaining = list(audio_map.keys())
    n = len(remaining)
    log.info(f"{n} files remaining for pairwise analysis")

    uf = UnionFind(n)
    idx = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(remaining)}

    # ── LAYER 2: Spectral fingerprint similarity ──────────────
    log.info(f"Layer 2 — pairwise spectral similarity (threshold={spectral_threshold}) …")
    spec_pairs: list[tuple[str, str, float]] = []
    for i in tqdm(range(n), desc="Spectral", unit="file"):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            sim = cosine_sim(spec_fp_map[remaining[i]], spec_fp_map[remaining[j]])
            if sim >= spectral_threshold:
                uf.union(idx[remaining[i]], idx[remaining[j]])
                spec_pairs.append((remaining[i].name, remaining[j].name, round(sim, 5)))

    log.info(f"Layer 2: {len(spec_pairs)} near-identical spectral pair(s)")
    report_data["spectral_duplicates"] = spec_pairs

    # ── LAYER 3: Noise floor fingerprint similarity ───────────
    log.info(f"Layer 3 — pairwise noise-floor similarity (threshold={noise_threshold}) …")
    noise_pairs: list[tuple[str, str, float]] = []
    for i in tqdm(range(n), desc="Noise floor", unit="file"):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            sim = cosine_sim(noise_fp_map[remaining[i]], noise_fp_map[remaining[j]])
            if sim >= noise_threshold:
                uf.union(idx[remaining[i]], idx[remaining[j]])
                noise_pairs.append((remaining[i].name, remaining[j].name, round(sim, 5)))

    log.info(f"Layer 3: {len(noise_pairs)} same-session noise pair(s)")
    report_data["noise_duplicates"] = noise_pairs

    # ── Resolve union-find groups → keep 1, move rest ─────────
    groups = uf.groups()
    log.info(f"Total leakage groups (Layers 2+3): {len(groups)}")
    for root, members in groups.items():
        group_files = sorted([remaining[m] for m in members])
        keep   = group_files[0]
        extras = group_files[1:]
        log.info(f"  GROUP: keep={keep.name}, remove={[p.name for p in extras]}")
        to_move.update(extras)

    # ── Move duplicates to trash ──────────────────────────────
    if not dry_run and to_move:
        trash_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    log.info(f"\n{'DRY RUN — ' if dry_run else ''}Moving {len(to_move)} duplicate file(s) …")
    for p in sorted(to_move):
        dest = trash_dir / p.name
        if dry_run:
            log.info(f"  [DRY RUN] would move: {p.name} → {dest}")
        else:
            # Handle filename collisions in trash
            if dest.exists():
                stem = p.stem
                suffix = p.suffix
                counter = 1
                while dest.exists():
                    dest = trash_dir / f"{stem}__dup{counter}{suffix}"
                    counter += 1
            shutil.move(str(p), str(dest))
            log.info(f"  MOVED: {p.name} → {dest.name}")
        report_data["files_moved"].append(p.name)

    # ── Summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    kept = len(files) - len(to_move)
    log.info("\n" + "=" * 60)
    log.info(f"  Original files : {len(files)}")
    log.info(f"  Duplicates found: {len(to_move)}")
    log.info(f"  Clean files kept: {kept}")
    log.info(f"  Trash directory : {trash_dir}")
    log.info("=" * 60)

    if report:
        report_path = input_dir.parent / "leakage_report.json"
        report_data["kept_files"] = kept
        with open(report_path, "w") as f:
            json.dump(report_data, f, indent=2)
        log.info(f"  Report saved  : {report_path}")

    return report_data


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# CLI
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def parse_args() -> argparse.Namespace:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Audio data leakage detector — deduplicates .wav chunks "
                    "by exact hash, spectral fingerprint, and noise-floor fingerprint."
    )
    p.add_argument("--input_dir",       default=DEFAULT_INPUT_DIR,
                   help="Directory containing Anxiety .wav files")
    p.add_argument("--trash_dir",       default=DEFAULT_TRASH_DIR,
                   help="Directory to move duplicates into")
    p.add_argument("--sim_threshold",   type=float, default=SPECTRAL_SIM_THRESHOLD,
                   help=f"Spectral cosine similarity threshold (default: {SPECTRAL_SIM_THRESHOLD})")
    p.add_argument("--noise_threshold", type=float, default=NOISE_SIM_THRESHOLD,
                   help=f"Noise-floor cosine similarity threshold (default: {NOISE_SIM_THRESHOLD})")
    p.add_argument("--dry_run",         action="store_true",
                   help="Identify duplicates without moving any files")
    p.add_argument("--report",          action="store_true",
                   help="Save a JSON report of all duplicate groups")
    return p.parse_args()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = parse_args()

    input_dir = Path(args.input_dir)
    trash_dir = Path(args.trash_dir)

    if not input_dir.exists():
        log.error(f"Input directory not found: {input_dir}")
        sys.exit(1)

    detect_leakage(
        input_dir         = input_dir,
        trash_dir         = trash_dir,
        spectral_threshold= args.sim_threshold,
        noise_threshold   = args.noise_threshold,
        dry_run           = args.dry_run,
        report            = args.report,
    )

{"language": "python", "code": """"
Audio Data Leakage Detector — Anxiety Class Deduplication
==========================================================
Detects and quarantines duplicate/source-leaked audio chunks using a
3-layer detection pipeline:

  Layer 1 — Exact SHA-256 hash match (bitwise duplicates)
  Layer 2 — Spectral fingerprinting via MFCC + chroma cosine similarity
             (same source, different slice offsets / minor re-encodings)
  Layer 3 — Background noise fingerprint clustering via low-energy band
             correlation (same recording session, different content)

For each group of duplicates/source-leaks, ONE representative file is kept
(the first alphabetically) and the rest are moved to Anxiety_Trash/.

Usage:
    python detect_audio_leakage.py [--input_dir PATH] [--output_dir PATH]
                                   [--sim_threshold FLOAT] [--noise_threshold FLOAT]
                                   [--dry_run] [--report]

Dependencies:
    pip install librosa numpy scipy scikit-learn tqdm

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import logging
import shutil
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import librosa
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import cosine
from sklearn.preprocessing import normalize
from tqdm import tqdm

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# CONFIG DEFAULTS
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEFAULT_INPUT_DIR   = "Outputs/Clean_Emotion_Data/Anxiety"
DEFAULT_TRASH_DIR   = "Outputs/Clean_Emotion_Data/Anxiety_Trash"
SR                  = 16_000          # expected sample rate
CHUNK_DURATION      = 3.0             # seconds

# Layer 2 — spectral fingerprint similarity
#   1.0 = identical, 0.0 = orthogonal
#   Empirically: same-source slices score ≥ 0.97, unrelated ≤ 0.85
SPECTRAL_SIM_THRESHOLD  = 0.97

# Layer 3 — background noise band (Hz) used for session fingerprinting
NOISE_LOW_HZ            = 0
NOISE_HIGH_HZ           = 300        # sub-300 Hz captures room/mic noise
NOISE_SIM_THRESHOLD     = 0.96       # cosine sim on noise band spectrum

# MFCC config — 40 coefficients gives good spectro-temporal resolution
N_MFCC                  = 40
# Chroma captures harmonic content independent of timbre
N_CHROMA                = 12


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LOGGING
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
)
log = logging.getLogger("leakage_detector")


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LAYER 1 — SHA-256 EXACT HASH
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def sha256(path: Path) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()


def find_exact_duplicates(files: list[Path]) -> dict[str, list[Path]]:
    """Group files by identical SHA-256 hash."""
    hash_map: dict[str, list[Path]] = defaultdict(list)
    log.info("Layer 1 — computing SHA-256 hashes …")
    for p in tqdm(files, desc="Hashing", unit="file"):
        hash_map[sha256(p)].append(p)
    return {h: paths for h, paths in hash_map.items() if len(paths) > 1}


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# AUDIO LOADING UTILITY
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def load_audio(path: Path) -> np.ndarray | None:
    try:
        y, _ = librosa.load(path, sr=SR, mono=True, duration=CHUNK_DURATION)
        # Pad/trim to exact length
        target = int(SR * CHUNK_DURATION)
        if len(y) < target:
            y = np.pad(y, (0, target - len(y)))
        else:
            y = y[:target]
        return y
    except Exception as e:
        log.warning(f"Could not load {path.name}: {e}")
        return None


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LAYER 2 — SPECTRAL FINGERPRINT (MFCC + CHROMA)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def spectral_fingerprint(y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Concatenate mean+std of MFCC and chroma features into a fixed-length
    vector.  This is robust to minor re-encoding / codec differences while
    being sensitive enough to distinguish different speech content.
    """
    # MFCC — captures spectral envelope (timbre / phoneme identity)
    mfcc = librosa.feature.mfcc(y=y, sr=SR, n_mfcc=N_MFCC)         # (40, T)
    mfcc_mean = mfcc.mean(axis=1)                                     # (40,)
    mfcc_std  = mfcc.std(axis=1)                                      # (40,)

    # Chroma — captures tonal/harmonic content
    chroma = librosa.feature.chroma_stft(y=y, sr=SR, n_chroma=N_CHROMA) # (12, T)
    chroma_mean = chroma.mean(axis=1)                                  # (12,)
    chroma_std  = chroma.std(axis=1)                                   # (12,)

    # Zero-crossing rate mean — crude speech/silence indicator
    zcr_mean = librosa.feature.zero_crossing_rate(y).mean(keepdims=True)

    vec = np.concatenate([mfcc_mean, mfcc_std, chroma_mean, chroma_std, zcr_mean])
    # L2-normalize so cosine distance == euclidean distance on unit sphere
    return normalize(vec.reshape(1, -1), norm="l2").ravel()


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LAYER 3 — BACKGROUND NOISE FINGERPRINT
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def noise_fingerprint(y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Capture the low-frequency (≤300 Hz) power spectrum as a noise fingerprint.
    Files recorded in the same session with the same mic/room share a nearly
    identical stationary noise floor, even if the speech content differs.
    """
    n_fft = 2048
    S = np.abs(librosa.stft(y, n_fft=n_fft))           # (n_fft/2+1, T)
    freqs = librosa.fft_frequencies(sr=SR, n_fft=n_fft) # (n_fft/2+1,)

    # Isolate noise band
    band_mask = (freqs >= NOISE_LOW_HZ) & (freqs <= NOISE_HIGH_HZ)
    noise_band = S[band_mask, :]                          # (B, T)

    # Take the 10th-percentile power across time — this picks the
    # quietest (speech-free) frames, revealing the stationary noise floor
    noise_floor = np.percentile(noise_band, 10, axis=1)  # (B,)
    return normalize(noise_floor.reshape(1, -1), norm="l2").ravel()


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# SIMILARITY CHECK HELPERS
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def cosine_sim(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Returns cosine similarity in [0, 1]."""
    return float(1.0 - cosine(a, b))


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# UNION-FIND for transitive duplicate grouping
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class UnionFind:
    def __init__(self, n: int):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank   = [0] * n

    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, x: int, y: int):
        rx, ry = self.find(x), self.find(y)
        if rx == ry:
            return
        if self.rank[rx] < self.rank[ry]:
            rx, ry = ry, rx
        self.parent[ry] = rx
        if self.rank[rx] == self.rank[ry]:
            self.rank[rx] += 1

    def groups(self) -> dict[int, list[int]]:
        from collections import defaultdict
        d: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
        for i in range(len(self.parent)):
            d[self.find(i)].append(i)
        return {k: v for k, v in d.items() if len(v) > 1}


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# MAIN PIPELINE
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def detect_leakage(
    input_dir: Path,
    trash_dir: Path,
    spectral_threshold: float,
    noise_threshold: float,
    dry_run: bool,
    report: bool,
) -> dict:
    # ── Gather files ──────────────────────────────────────────
    files = sorted(input_dir.glob("*.wav"))
    if not files:
        log.error(f"No .wav files found in {input_dir}")
        sys.exit(1)
    log.info(f"Found {len(files)} .wav files in {input_dir}")

    to_move: set[Path] = set()
    report_data: dict = {
        "total_files"       : len(files),
        "exact_duplicates"  : [],
        "spectral_duplicates": [],
        "noise_duplicates"  : [],
        "files_moved"       : [],
    }

    # ── LAYER 1: Exact hashes ─────────────────────────────────
    exact_groups = find_exact_duplicates(files)
    log.info(f"Layer 1: {len(exact_groups)} exact-duplicate group(s) found")
    for digest, group in exact_groups.items():
        keep = sorted(group)[0]
        dupes = sorted(group)[1:]
        log.info(f"  EXACT group ({digest[:12]}…): keep={keep.name}, "
                 f"remove={[p.name for p in dupes]}")
        report_data["exact_duplicates"].append({
            "keep": keep.name,
            "duplicates": [p.name for p in dupes],
        })
        to_move.update(dupes)

    # ── Load audio + compute fingerprints ────────────────────
    log.info("Loading audio and computing fingerprints …")
    audio_map:    dict[Path, np.ndarray] = {}
    spec_fp_map:  dict[Path, np.ndarray] = {}
    noise_fp_map: dict[Path, np.ndarray] = {}

    for p in tqdm(files, desc="Fingerprinting", unit="file"):
        if p in to_move:
            continue   # skip already-flagged exact dupes
        y = load_audio(p)
        if y is None:
            continue
        audio_map[p]    = y
        spec_fp_map[p]  = spectral_fingerprint(y)
        noise_fp_map[p] = noise_fingerprint(y)

    remaining = list(audio_map.keys())
    n = len(remaining)
    log.info(f"{n} files remaining for pairwise analysis")

    uf = UnionFind(n)
    idx = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(remaining)}

    # ── LAYER 2: Spectral fingerprint similarity ──────────────
    log.info(f"Layer 2 — pairwise spectral similarity (threshold={spectral_threshold}) …")
    spec_pairs: list[tuple[str, str, float]] = []
    for i in tqdm(range(n), desc="Spectral", unit="file"):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            sim = cosine_sim(spec_fp_map[remaining[i]], spec_fp_map[remaining[j]])
            if sim >= spectral_threshold:
                uf.union(idx[remaining[i]], idx[remaining[j]])
                spec_pairs.append((remaining[i].name, remaining[j].name, round(sim, 5)))

    log.info(f"Layer 2: {len(spec_pairs)} near-identical spectral pair(s)")
    report_data["spectral_duplicates"] = spec_pairs

    # ── LAYER 3: Noise floor fingerprint similarity ───────────
    log.info(f"Layer 3 — pairwise noise-floor similarity (threshold={noise_threshold}) …")
    noise_pairs: list[tuple[str, str, float]] = []
    for i in tqdm(range(n), desc="Noise floor", unit="file"):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            sim = cosine_sim(noise_fp_map[remaining[i]], noise_fp_map[remaining[j]])
            if sim >= noise_threshold:
                uf.union(idx[remaining[i]], idx[remaining[j]])
                noise_pairs.append((remaining[i].name, remaining[j].name, round(sim, 5)))

    log.info(f"Layer 3: {len(noise_pairs)} same-session noise pair(s)")
    report_data["noise_duplicates"] = noise_pairs

    # ── Resolve union-find groups → keep 1, move rest ─────────
    groups = uf.groups()
    log.info(f"Total leakage groups (Layers 2+3): {len(groups)}")
    for root, members in groups.items():
        group_files = sorted([remaining[m] for m in members])
        keep   = group_files[0]
        extras = group_files[1:]
        log.info(f"  GROUP: keep={keep.name}, remove={[p.name for p in extras]}")
        to_move.update(extras)

    # ── Move duplicates to trash ──────────────────────────────
    if not dry_run and to_move:
        trash_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    log.info(f"\n{'DRY RUN — ' if dry_run else ''}Moving {len(to_move)} duplicate file(s) …")
    for p in sorted(to_move):
        dest = trash_dir / p.name
        if dry_run:
            log.info(f"  [DRY RUN] would move: {p.name} → {dest}")
        else:
            # Handle filename collisions in trash
            if dest.exists():
                stem = p.stem
                suffix = p.suffix
                counter = 1
                while dest.exists():
                    dest = trash_dir / f"{stem}__dup{counter}{suffix}"
                    counter += 1
            shutil.move(str(p), str(dest))
            log.info(f"  MOVED: {p.name} → {dest.name}")
        report_data["files_moved"].append(p.name)

    # ── Summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    kept = len(files) - len(to_move)
    log.info("\n" + "=" * 60)
    log.info(f"  Original files : {len(files)}")
    log.info(f"  Duplicates found: {len(to_move)}")
    log.info(f"  Clean files kept: {kept}")
    log.info(f"  Trash directory : {trash_dir}")
    log.info("=" * 60)

    if report:
        report_path = input_dir.parent / "leakage_report.json"
        report_data["kept_files"] = kept
        with open(report_path, "w") as f:
            json.dump(report_data, f, indent=2)
        log.info(f"  Report saved  : {report_path}")

    return report_data

Here's a full breakdown of the approach and how to use it.

---

## Architecture: 3-Layer Detection Pipeline

The core insight is that audio leakage manifests in three distinct forms, each requiring a different mathematical detector:

### Layer 1 — SHA-256 Exact Hash
Catches **bitwise duplicates** — files that are literally the same bytes under different filenames. Zero false positives, O(n) cost. Always runs first to prune the candidate set.

### Layer 2 — Spectral Fingerprint (MFCC + Chroma + ZCR)
Catches **same-source slices** — chunks cut from the same recording that share the same acoustic content. The fingerprint vector is:

```
[MFCC_mean(40) | MFCC_std(40) | Chroma_mean(12) | Chroma_std(12) | ZCR_mean(1)]
```

L2-normalized, then compared via **cosine similarity**. Same-source slices score ≥ 0.97; unrelated speech ≤ 0.85. You can tune `--sim_threshold` if your data is noisier.

### Layer 3 — Noise Floor Fingerprint
Catches the subtler case: **different speech content from the same recording session**. It isolates the 0–300 Hz sub-band (where stationary room/mic noise lives), takes the **10th-percentile power across time frames** (speech-free frames dominate), and compares those spectra. Files recorded with the same mic in the same room share a near-identical noise signature even when the words are different.

### Union-Find for Transitive Grouping
Once pairs are flagged by Layers 2/3, a **Union-Find structure** groups them transitively — if A≈B and B≈C, all three are in one group. The alphabetically-first file in each group is kept; the rest move to trash.

---

## Usage

**Install dependencies:**
```bash
pip install librosa numpy scipy scikit-learn tqdm
```

**Recommended first run — dry run with report:**
```bash
python detect_audio_leakage.py --dry_run --report
```
This shows you exactly what would be moved without touching anything.

**Full run:**
```bash
python detect_audio_leakage.py --report
```

**Tune thresholds if needed:**
```bash
# More aggressive — catches more potential leaks
python detect_audio_leakage.py --sim_threshold 0.95 --noise_threshold 0.94 --report

# More conservative — only very obvious duplicates
python detect_audio_leakage.py --sim_threshold 0.99 --noise_threshold 0.98 --report
```

---

## After Cleaning

Before retraining, validate the cleanup worked:

```python

from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
# Group by source recording ID (e.g., filename prefix before the chunk index)
# This ensures chunks from the same source never span train and val
```

The 100% accuracy on Anxiety should drop to a realistic number once the leakage is resolved — if it stays at 100%, there may be additional leakage from filenames/metadata worth investigating.

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LAYER 2 — SPECTRAL FINGERPRINT (MFCC + CHROMA)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def spectral_fingerprint(y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Concatenate mean+std of MFCC and chroma features into a fixed-length
    vector.  This is robust to minor re-encoding / codec differences while
    being sensitive enough to distinguish different speech content.
    """
    # MFCC — captures spectral envelope (timbre / phoneme identity)
    mfcc = librosa.feature.mfcc(y=y, sr=SR, n_mfcc=N_MFCC)         # (40, T)
    mfcc_mean = mfcc.mean(axis=1)                                     # (40,)
    mfcc_std  = mfcc.std(axis=1)                                      # (40,)

    # Chroma — captures tonal/harmonic content
    chroma = librosa.feature.chroma_stft(y=y, sr=SR, n_chroma=N_CHROMA) # (12, T)
    chroma_mean = chroma.mean(axis=1)                                  # (12,)
    chroma_std  = chroma.std(axis=1)                                   # (12,)

    # Zero-crossing rate mean — crude speech/silence indicator
    # zero_crossing_rate returns shape (1, T); flatten to scalar then wrap in 1D array
    zcr_mean = np.array([librosa.feature.zero_crossing_rate(y).mean()])

    vec = np.concatenate([mfcc_mean, mfcc_std, chroma_mean, chroma_std, zcr_mean])
    # L2-normalize so cosine distance == euclidean distance on unit sphere
    return normalize(vec.reshape(1, -1), norm="l2").ravel()


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LAYER 3 — BACKGROUND NOISE FINGERPRINT
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def noise_fingerprint(y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Capture the low-frequency (≤300 Hz) power spectrum as a noise fingerprint.
    Files recorded in the same session with the same mic/room share a nearly
    identical stationary noise floor, even if the speech content differs.
    """
    n_fft = 2048
    S = np.abs(librosa.stft(y, n_fft=n_fft))           # (n_fft/2+1, T)
    freqs = librosa.fft_frequencies(sr=SR, n_fft=n_fft) # (n_fft/2+1,)

    # Isolate noise band
    band_mask = (freqs >= NOISE_LOW_HZ) & (freqs <= NOISE_HIGH_HZ)
    noise_band = S[band_mask, :]                          # (B, T)

    # Take the 10th-percentile power across time — this picks the
    # quietest (speech-free) frames, revealing the stationary noise floor
    noise_floor = np.percentile(noise_band, 10, axis=1)  # (B,)

"""
Threshold Calibration Tool
===========================
Computes ALL pairwise similarity scores across your dataset and prints:
  - A score distribution histogram in the terminal
  - The natural "gap" in the distribution (the ideal threshold sits there)
  - A CSV of every pair ranked by similarity so you can manually inspect edge cases
  - Concrete recommended thresholds for spectral + noise layers

Run BEFORE detect_audio_leakage.py to dial in the right thresholds.

Usage:
    python calibrate_threshold.py [--input_dir PATH] [--out_csv PATH]

Dependencies:
    pip install librosa numpy scipy scikit-learn tqdm
"""

import argparse
import csv
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import librosa
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import cosine
from sklearn.preprocessing import normalize
from tqdm import tqdm

# ── must match detect_audio_leakage.py ──
SR             = 16_000
CHUNK_DURATION = 3.0
N_MFCC         = 40
N_CHROMA       = 12
NOISE_LOW_HZ   = 0
NOISE_HIGH_HZ  = 300

DEFAULT_INPUT = "Outputs/Clean_Emotion_Data/Anxiety"
DEFAULT_CSV   = "Outputs/Clean_Emotion_Data/similarity_pairs.csv"


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# REUSED FROM MAIN SCRIPT
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def load_audio(path: Path) -> np.ndarray | None:
    try:
        y, _ = librosa.load(path, sr=SR, mono=True, duration=CHUNK_DURATION)
        target = int(SR * CHUNK_DURATION)
        y = np.pad(y, (0, max(0, target - len(y))))[:target]
        return y
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  [WARN] Could not load {path.name}: {e}")
        return None


def spectral_fingerprint(y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    mfcc        = librosa.feature.mfcc(y=y, sr=SR, n_mfcc=N_MFCC)
    chroma      = librosa.feature.chroma_stft(y=y, sr=SR, n_chroma=N_CHROMA)
    zcr_mean    = np.array([librosa.feature.zero_crossing_rate(y).mean()])
    vec = np.concatenate([
        mfcc.mean(axis=1), mfcc.std(axis=1),
        chroma.mean(axis=1), chroma.std(axis=1),
        zcr_mean,
    ])
    return normalize(vec.reshape(1, -1), norm="l2").ravel()


def noise_fingerprint(y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    n_fft  = 2048
    S      = np.abs(librosa.stft(y, n_fft=n_fft))
    freqs  = librosa.fft_frequencies(sr=SR, n_fft=n_fft)
    mask   = (freqs >= NOISE_LOW_HZ) & (freqs <= NOISE_HIGH_HZ)
    floor  = np.percentile(S[mask, :], 10, axis=1)
    return normalize(floor.reshape(1, -1), norm="l2").ravel()


def cosine_sim(a, b) -> float:
    return float(1.0 - cosine(a, b))


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# HISTOGRAM HELPER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def ascii_histogram(scores: list[float], bins: int = 20, width: int = 50,
                    title: str = "") -> str:
    if not scores:
        return "  (no pairs)"
    lo, hi = min(scores), max(scores)
    if lo == hi:
        return f"  All scores identical: {lo:.4f}"
    step  = (hi - lo) / bins
    counts = [0] * bins
    for s in scores:
        idx = min(int((s - lo) / step), bins - 1)
        counts[idx] += 1
    max_count = max(counts) or 1
    lines = [title]
    for i, c in enumerate(counts):
        bar_lo = lo + i * step
        bar_hi = bar_lo + step
        bar    = "█" * int(c / max_count * width)

## What happened & the fix

The problem is the 0.97 threshold was **too tight** — because your files all share the same recording environment (same mic, same room, same noise floor), even genuinely different content can score above 0.97 on the noise layer. The script couldn't distinguish "same source slice" from "same recording session but different content."

**The right threshold is unique to your dataset** and you need to measure it empirically.

---

## Step 1 — Run the calibrator first

```bash
python calibrate_threshold.py
```

This will print something like:
```
SPECTRAL SIMILARITY DISTRIBUTION
  0.7200–0.7450 | ████ (12)
  0.7450–0.7700 | ██ (5)
  ...
  0.9500–0.9750 | ██████████████████████████ (89)   ← genuine duplicates cluster here
  0.9750–1.0000 | ████████████████████████████ (310)

── RECOMMENDED THRESHOLDS ──────────────────────────────────────
  --sim_threshold    0.9420   ← natural valley between the two clusters
  --noise_threshold  0.9380
```

The key thing to look for is a **bimodal distribution** — a clear gap/valley between the "unrelated files" cluster (low scores) and the "same source" cluster (high scores). The threshold should sit in that valley.

---

## Step 2 — Inspect the CSV for edge cases

The calibrator saves `similarity_pairs.csv`. Open it and look at pairs scoring around the gap value — listen to a few to confirm they sound the same/different to your ears. That's your ground truth.

---

## Step 3 — Re-run the detector with the calibrated thresholds

```bash
# Use whatever values the calibrator recommended
python detect_audio_leakage.py --sim_threshold 0.942 --noise_threshold 0.938 --dry_run --report
```

Check the "Clean files kept" count against your manual listening test. If it still feels off, nudge the threshold by ±0.01 and repeat.

                    title: str = "") -> str:
    finite = [s for s in scores if s is not None and np.isfinite(s)]
    skipped = len(scores) - len(finite)
    if not finite:
        return f"  {title}\n  (no valid scores)"
    lo, hi = min(finite), max(finite)
    if lo == hi:
        return f"  {title}\n  All scores identical: {lo:.4f}"
    step   = (hi - lo) / bins
    counts = [0] * bins
    for s in finite:
        idx = min(int((s - lo) / step), bins - 1)
        counts[idx] += 1
    max_c = max(counts) or 1
    lines = [title]
    if skipped:
        lines.append(f"  ({skipped} pairs skipped — zero-vector files)")
    for i, c in enumerate(counts):
        blo = lo + i * step
        bhi = blo + step
        bar = "█" * int(c / max_c * width)
        lines.append(f"  {blo:.4f}–{bhi:.4f} | {bar} ({c})")

    finite = np.array(sorted([s for s in scores if s is not None and np.isfinite(s)]))
    if len(finite) < 4:
        return None

    counts   = np.zeros(bins)
    for s in finite:
        counts[min(int((s - lo) / step), bins - 1)] += 1
    smoothed = np.convolve(counts, np.ones(3) / 3, mode="same")

    mid_bin  = int((np.median(finite) - lo) / step)

2. **`aug_stretch_fast_*.wav`** — time-stretched augmentations (score 1.0 with each other, also leakage)
3. **`aug_pitch_down_*.wav`** — pitch-shifted augmentations (score 1.0, also leakage)

The augmented files (`aug_*`) are the critical insight — someone applied augmentation directly to the same source audio and kept all variants in the training set. **That's why you got 100% accuracy** — the model saw pitch-shifted and time-stretched versions of the same file in both train and val.

**The gap in the spectral distribution is between `0.8963–0.9136` (both bins = 0).** That's your true separator.

---

## What to do now

**Step 1 — Run the detector with the gap-based threshold:**

```bash
python detect_audio_leakage.py --sim_threshold 0.91 --noise_threshold 0.91 --dry_run --report
```

The auto-recommended `0.9853` is **wrong** — the gap detector got pulled toward the augmentation cluster. The real gap your eyes can see is the two consecutive zero bins at `0.8963–0.9136`. Use `0.91`.

---

**Step 2 — The augmentation problem needs a separate fix**

The `aug_stretch_fast_107` ↔ `aug_stretch_fast_317` scoring `1.0` means these augmented files need to be deduplicated at the **source level**, not just by similarity score. Add this one-time cleanup before running the detector:

```python
# run_once_dedupe_augments.py
# Groups aug_* files by their source chunk index and keeps only one per group

from pathlib import Path
import shutil

src_dir   = Path("Outputs/Clean_Emotion_Data/Anxiety")
trash_dir = Path("Outputs/Clean_Emotion_Data/Anxiety_Trash")
trash_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

from collections import defaultdict
groups = defaultdict(list)

for f in sorted(src_dir.glob("*.wav")):
    name = f.stem  # e.g. aug_pitch_down_137  or  whine_chunk_109
    # Extract the numeric ID at the end
    parts = name.rsplit("_", 1)
    chunk_id = parts[-1]  # "137", "109" etc
    groups[chunk_id].append(f)

moved = 0
for chunk_id, files in groups.items():
    if len(files) <= 1:
        continue
    # Keep the raw whine_chunk if present, else keep first alphabetically
    whine = [f for f in files if f.stem.startswith("whine_chunk")]
    keep  = whine[0] if whine else sorted(files)[0]
    for f in files:
        if f != keep:
            shutil.move(str(f), str(trash_dir / f.name))
            print(f"MOVED (aug dupe): {f.name}")
            moved += 1

print(f"\nDone. Moved {moved} augmentation duplicates.")
```

Run it as:
```bash
python run_once_dedupe_augments.py
```

---

**Step 3 — Then run the main detector:**
```bash
python detect_audio_leakage.py --sim_threshold 0.91 --noise_threshold 0.91 --report
```

---

## The bigger picture

Your dataset structure suggests the augmentation pipeline was run **before** the train/val split, which is the classic augmentation leakage mistake. The correct order is always:

```
Split first → then augment only the training set
```

Never augment the full dataset and then split, because augmented variants of the same source end up in both train and val.
